title: Microbial dormancy under freeze–thaw cycling regulates alpine soil responses to warming
abstract: Abstract Microbial regulation of soil carbon cycling in cold ecosystems remains poorly constrained in Earth system models, largely due to limited observations and unresolved mechanisms. Here, we develop a freeze–thaw-enabled microbial-ecological model (MEND-FT) and integrate it with multi-year whole-soil warming experiments in an alpine meadow on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau to investigate warming effects on soil carbon dynamics from microbial physiology to ecosystem processes. This experiment-model framework reveals amplified warming impacts during non-growing seasons, an underexplored period, driven by reduced frozen depths ( − 43 cm), prolonged thaw duration ( + 38 days), and widespread microbial dormancy. MEND-FT reproduces observed minimal enzyme responses and resolves seasonal microbial activity shifts via dormancy regulation, mechanisms absent from previous analyses. We further refine microbial carbon use efficiency estimates to align with ecosystem-level benchmarks, showing slight but persistent declines under warming. Long-term simulations suggest that the modest soil carbon loss ( − 2.2%) co-occurs with increased microbial biomass and enhanced oxidase activity, consistent with freeze-thaw-induced microbial physiological regulation rather than substrate depletion alone. Together, these findings provide compelling evidence that microbial dormancy-resuscitation dynamics govern soil carbon responses to climate and environmental changes, offering a scalable and transferable mechanistic framework for improving predictions of soil carbon persistence and greenhouse gas emissions across diverse biomes.
problem: Existing ecosystem models inadequately predict soil carbon responses to warming in cold regions because they largely overlook the critical role of microbial dormancy and resuscitation dynamics during seasonal freeze-thaw cycles, leading to poorly constrained predictions.
method: We develop a freeze-thaw-enabled microbial-ecological model (MEND-FT) and integrate it with multi-year warming experiments to investigate how microbial dormancy under freeze-thaw cycling regulates alpine soil carbon responses to warming.
task: The task is to use a freeze-thaw-enabled microbial model integrated with multi-year warming experiments to investigate how microbial dormancy under freeze-thaw cycling regulates alpine soil carbon responses to warming.
innovation: By developing a freeze-thaw-enabled microbial model (MEND-FT) and integrating it with alpine warming experiments, this paper reveals that microbial dormancy-resuscitation dynamics are a key mechanism regulating soil carbon responses to warming, particularly by amplifying impacts during the non-growing season.

We derived the freeze-thaw processes using daily soil temperature and moisture data based on the Stefan solution 31, 32, and integrated them into the MEND-FT model using a scaling factor, ALTscalar, defined as the ratio of the thawed soil depth to the total soil depth (Fig. 1). The thermal conductivity (k) of the upper frozen or thawed soils was calculated as functions of soil moisture, bulk density, soil type, and organic matter content, following Johansen 70, which is also applied in CLM4.5. Soil temperature at 5 cm was used to calculate the freezing and thawing indices (I(t)), as it has smaller diurnal variation compared to surface soil temperature and provides a consistent periodic relationship with time 32. We assumed that freezing or thawing fronts start only at the soil surface and that no more than two freezing or thawing fronts exist simultaneously.
